specAnchors.text: understand reasons for the trends for Group 7 elements in: i melting and boiling temperatures and physical state at room temperature ii electronegativity iii reactivity down the group

primer.text: Descend Group 7 and everything shifts: colours deepen, boiling points climb, and the pull each atom exerts on electrons weakens. This note walks the ladder, explains volatility through intermolecular attractions, and shows why smaller halogens grab electrons - and react - more eagerly than their heavier cousins.

modules.title: Appearance and volatility down Group 7
modules.opening: The halogens are the Group 7 non-metals, and their look and their ease of evaporation both shift steadily as you descend. This lesson names the colour ladder, defines volatility through boiling point, and ties both trends to the growing electron clouds of the heavier atoms.
keyPoints: The Group 7 elements are the halogens, used as disinfectants, flame retardants and antiseptics.
Halogen colours darken steadily from fluorine through iodine going down the group.
Volatility means how readily a liquid evaporates, and a volatile substance boils low.
Melting and boiling points rise down the group, so volatility falls and iodine is the least volatile halogen.

low.restatement: Halogen colours deepen from pale fluorine to dark iodine, while boiling points climb, so the lightest halogen evaporates most easily and the heaviest least.
low.analogy: Think of a family of paints that darkens with every shade down the chart, and pots that get harder and harder to pour out as you move down.
low.examPointer: Quote the direction of both trends explicitly - darker colours and falling volatility down the group - because stating the direction earns the mark.

medium.restatement: Darkening colours and rising melting and boiling points both trace back to more electrons per molecule: bigger electron clouds give stronger induced dipole-dipole attractions that must be overcome to separate the simple molecular halogens.
medium.analogy: Heavier diatomic molecules are like stickier droplets - more contact area of weak attraction means more heat needed to shake them apart into gas.
medium.examPointer: Link colour depth and volatility to intermolecular attraction strength in one sentence when a question asks for an explanation, not just the observation.

modules.title: Simple molecular structure and electronegativity
sourceHeadings: Trend in melting and boiling points
modules.opening: Halogen crystals melt easily and the group's pull on bonding electrons fades as atoms grow. This lesson links both facts to structure: simple molecules held by weak induced dipole forces, and outer shells sinking ever further behind added screening layers.
keyPoints: Halogens are non-metals existing as diatomic molecules with simple molecular structures.
London dispersion forces between diatomic molecules are weak, explaining the group's low melting points.
Electronegativity measures how strongly an atom attracts electrons in a covalent bond.
Electronegativity decreases down the group as atomic radius and shielding grow, so oxidising power also falls.

low.restatement: Each halogen is a pair of atoms joined covalently; between the pairs sit weak attractions, so little heat separates them. Larger halogens attract incoming electrons less because the outer shell sits further out behind more shielding.
low.analogy: Each molecule is a tiny magnet pair with weak glue between pairs; the bigger atoms are like magnets wrapped in extra foam, their pull felt less at the surface.
low.examPointer: Name the attraction as induced dipole-induced dipole (London dispersion) and name shielding plus increasing atomic radius when explaining the electronegativity fall.

medium.restatement: Instantaneous electron imbalances in one non-polar molecule induce opposite dipoles in neighbours; more electrons make both the instantaneous and induced dipoles larger. The same growing radius and shielding that weaken electron capture also weaken electronegativity and oxidising ability.
medium.analogy: Crowded footballs flick neighbouring balls as they wobble; the bigger the ball's surface charge flicker, the stronger the flick it delivers.
medium.examPointer: Distinguish the two trends: melting/boiling rise because intermolecular force grows, while electronegativity and oxidising power fall because nuclear pull at the outer shell weakens.

modules.title: Reactivity as oxidising agents and the hydrogen test
modules.opening: A halogen atom normally ends up as a 1- ion, which makes every halogen an oxidising agent. This lesson follows that reduction, shows why the bigger atoms do it worse, and uses the hydrogen reaction as the vivid vigour test of the trend.
keyPoints: A reacting halogen atom gains one electron to form a 1- ion, so the halogen is reduced and acts as an oxidising agent.
The oxidation number falls from 0 to -1 when a halogen reacts to form its halide.
Larger halogen atoms attract the incoming electron less strongly, so reactivity decreases down the group.
Reactions with hydrogen gas become less vigorous down the group, giving the trend a visible demonstration.

low.restatement: Each halogen picks up one electron, dropping its oxidation number from 0 to -1; the smaller halogens do this eagerly, the larger ones reluctantly, and the hydrogen reactions slow down in step.
low.analogy: Small combs pick up paper crisply; larger, more shielded combs barely lift it - the halogens' electron capture weakens the same way.
low.examPointer: Write the half-equation X + e- -> X- and state the 0 to -1 oxidation-number fall when asked why halogens act as oxidising agents.

medium.restatement: Electron gain is reduction, so the halogen oxidises whatever supplies the electron. The gain is easiest when the incoming electron meets little shielding and short distance to the nucleus, so reactivity tracks electronegativity down the group, and the vigour with hydrogen demonstrates it.
medium.analogy: A narrow funnel pours quickly; a wide, foam-lined funnel slows every pour - added shells slow the electron's arrival just the same.
medium.examPointer: Link reactivity to oxidising power and quote the hydrogen-reaction trend as evidence in a 'describe and explain' answer.

glossary.definition: A Group 7 non-metal that exists as a diatomic simple molecular substance and readily gains one electron to form a halide ion.
The ease with which a substance evaporates, tracked by a low boiling point.
The weakest intermolecular attraction, arising when a fleeting electron imbalance in one molecule induces an opposite dipole in a neighbour.
The strength with which an atom attracts the shared electron pair in a covalent bond.
The ability of a species to take electrons from another species, oxidising it while being reduced itself.
